demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another. This appraisal is much more characteristic of interpersonal violence or sexual trauma, and it does not fit well with the rest of this profile, which centers on danger, guilt/humiliation, physical reactivity, and accident-related pain memories.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
issues.explanation: 'Being forced to do something' is a coercion/interpersonal-control trigger that lacks a clear clinical link to the reported trauma of accidentally injuring someone. The other triggers and memory items suggest accident reminders and bodily pain cues; this item pulls toward a different trauma theme and is not supported by the appraisals or memory content.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons
issues.explanation: Avoidance of military/police uniforms or weapons is not well grounded in the rest of the profile for an accidental-injury trauma. There are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items involving authority figures, weapons, or armed contexts, so this avoidance strategy appears to target a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the report.

issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: The threat profile is not well anchored to the indexed trauma. For accidentally causing serious injury to another, the rest of the profile centers on driving/crash reminders, guilt, pain, and sensory trauma memories. By contrast, 'Threat in Delays' and especially 'Door and Lock Checking' suggest a broader vigilance/checking presentation that is difficult to connect to the accident-specific trigger and memory content.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Within the Threat node, the items mix trauma-linked reactivity ('strong physical reactions when reminded') with generalized danger expectancy in ordinary delays and home-security checking. That combination can occur clinically, but here the latter two items are not supported by corresponding triggers, memories, or appraisals, making the node internally and cross-node less coherent.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: Door/window checking implies an ongoing interpersonal/home-intrusion danger theme that is not well supported by the trauma type (accidentally causing serious injury to another) or by the rest of the profile, which is otherwise centered on accident reminders, guilt, and vehicle-related distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place
issues.explanation: 'The world is a dangerous place' is possible after trauma, but here it pulls the formulation toward diffuse external danger rather than the profile's dominant accident-related guilt/shame theme. In combination with door/window checking, it creates a second threat system not well integrated with the other selected items.

vignette:
Margaret Calloway, a 60-year-old divorced politician of Irish-American descent, presents with a PCL-5 score of 68 following a motor vehicle accident in which she was the driver and in which a pedestrian sustained serious injuries. She has been serving in a state legislative role for over a decade, a position that has always demanded a high tolerance for public pressure and interpersonal conflict. She sought help only after her office staff raised concerns about her performance, and she arrived at the intake appointment visibly composed but effortfully so - the manner of a woman long practiced at projecting control.

The incident occurred approximately fourteen months ago on a wet November evening. Margaret was driving herself home from a late committee session, fatigued and preoccupied with the day's proceedings. At an intersection she knew well, she failed to see a man stepping from between parked cars and struck him at low speed. The impact was not catastrophic by some measures - he survived - but the sound was. A sharp, dense thud followed immediately by the man's cry, high and animal, and then her own scream as she braked. She remembers the particular way her neck snapped forward against the seatbelt and the radiating ache that followed. She remembers the shouting - her own, bystanders', eventually emergency responders - layered and disorienting against the hiss of rain. She remained at the scene, shaking, until the ambulance came. The man suffered a fractured pelvis and spent months in rehabilitation. Margaret was not charged. This, she has come to believe, made everything worse.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret found herself unable to account for what she had done. She had been driving that road for years. She had been careful, she had always been careful, and yet she was certain the accident had happened because of some essential carelessness in her character - an inattention she had simply never been caught in before. She would never forgive herself for not having braked sooner, for not having seen him, for not having taken a different route. The public nature of her role compounded her sense of exposure: a brief local news item had named her, and she had come to feel permanently marked by it, humiliated in a way that no professional achievement could reach.

Her avoidance developed gradually, in the way of habits that seem reasonable at the time. She stopped driving within the first month, arranging for staff to transport her to legislative sessions. Within a few months she had stopped being a passenger in cars whenever she could avoid it, citing scheduling flexibility to colleagues who asked. The consequence has been significant: a politician who once prided herself on constituent visibility now declines town hall events in distant districts, citing workload. Her chief of staff has quietly noted that she has missed three regional appearances in the past quarter. Margaret has told herself this is temporary.

Inside the chamber and in committee rooms, the difficulties are subtler but accumulating. When debate grows heated and voices rise - as they reliably do in her line of work - Margaret feels her body respond before her mind catches up: a flush of heat, a tightening across her chest, a sudden difficulty tracking what is being said. She has found herself losing the thread of arguments she has made dozens of times, sitting through votes with a concentration that feels like it is being held together by will alone. She avoids any situation that might generate strong feeling, including, she admits quietly, the celebratory dinners her party holds after legislative wins. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to feel anything at full volume, something would break that she would not be able to repair.

When she tries to deliberately recall the accident in order to account for it, the memory resists her - it will not come in an ordered way when she reaches for it. But it arrives unbidden: the sound of the impact, heard again from inside her skull; the ache in her neck reanimating without warning. What finally brought her to seek help was not the avoidance or the sleeplessness but a moment in committee when a colleague shouted across the floor and Margaret's hands began to shake visibly. She is most afraid, she says, that she is no longer fit for her role. What she hopes for, though she offers this carefully, is to stop feeling like a person who causes harm simply by moving through the world.
